clue.text: Understatement unusual in T. S. Eliot

indicators.note: unusual tells us the letters of the poet's name are put into an unusual order

explanation.surface: A remark that the poet T. S. Eliot seldom went in for understatement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' is the anagram signal: the seven letters of T S ELIOT are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names the rhetorical figure of deliberate understatement, such as saying 'not bad' to mean good.

clue.text: Youngster joining a highly principled person in strike

parts.note: a lamb is a young sheep, a youngster
St is the abbreviation for saint, a person of high principle

explanation.surface: A young worker teams up with an idealist to go on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike' looks like industrial action, but the definition is the verb to hit hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To lambast is to beat or thrash, so to strike.

clue.text: Present with race game

parts.note: a tip is a small present of money
and means with, together with
a run is a race

explanation.surface: A gift given with a racing contest.
explanation.walkthrough: TIP AND RUN is an informal form of cricket in which the batter must run whenever the bat touches the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a children's informal game of cricket where any contact forces a run.

clue.text: Such long hair some actresses have!

indicators.note: some that actresses have points to letters held within the word itself
some that actresses have points to letters held within the word itself

explanation.surface: An admiring remark about the lengthy locks of certain actresses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' and 'have' point to the letters inside 'actresses'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tress is a long lock of hair.

clue.text: See star pick plant

parts.note: the Sun is our star
the flower of something is the pick, the best of it

explanation.surface: An instruction to watch a celebrity choose a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is an imperative link word inviting the reader to look. 'pick' reads as choose, but it is the noun, the best part, as in the flower of youth.
explanation.definitionFit: The sunflower is a tall plant with large yellow heads that turn towards the light.

clue.text: Sailors trick old copper and escape

parts.note: ABs are able seamen, so sailors in the plural
to con someone is to trick them
D stood for the old penny, a copper coin of pre-decimal British money

explanation.surface: A gang of sailors swindle an elderly policeman and make a run for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old copper' looks like a retired policeman, but it is the old penny, a copper coin abbreviated D before British decimalisation in 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: To abscond is to run away secretly, typically to evade arrest, so it is to escape.

clue.text: A woman accepting it shows goodwill

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so one word holds another

parts.note: Amy is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman who agrees to something displays kindness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A woman' looks like an article plus a noun, but it is one name; 'accepting' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Amity is friendship and friendly relations, a state of goodwill.

clue.text: Firm making place secure

parts.note: stead means place, as in instead
fast means firmly fixed, secure

explanation.surface: A company that makes buildings safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company, but it is the adjective meaning resolute.
explanation.definitionFit: Steadfast means resolute and unwavering, firm.

clue.text: Starts to write in very large letters

indicators.note: in places one word inside another

parts.note: OS, for outsize, are the letters marking very large clothes
to pen is to write

explanation.surface: Someone begins writing in huge capitals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very large letters' reads as big handwriting, but it is the outsize label on clothes; 'in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Opens and starts both mean begins.

clue.text: Slough appears to be hopeless

definitions.meaning: the Slough of ... is the bog of despair in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, so slough means a mire of dejection
to lose hope, to be in despair

explanation.surface: The English town of Slough looks like a lost cause.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is a town west of London, often mocked; here it is the bog in Bunyan's allegory. 'appears to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is dejection, the bog of despair; as a verb it means to lose heart.

clue.text: Sugar-producer's a soft-hearted man

indicators.note: hearted says a letter is placed at the heart of the word for man

parts.note: a man is a male
P, piano, is the musical abbreviation for soft

explanation.surface: A gentle, kind-hearted man is said to be a provider of sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soft-hearted' reads as kind, but splits into P (soft) placed in the heart of MALE. The 's after the definition stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The sugar maple tree is tapped for sap that is boiled down into syrup and sugar.

clue.text: Lionesses moving around without a sound

indicators.note: moving around tells us the letters of the big cats' word shift about into new places

explanation.surface: Big cats prowl about in perfect silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving around' is the anagram signal, rearranging the nine letters of LIONESSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Something noiseless makes no noise at all, so it is silent.

clue.text: She's a fair target for shy people

definitions.text: She's a fair target for shy people

parts.words: She's a fair target for shy people
parts.note: a fair is a fairground, and to shy is to throw: the clue describes the female figure at a British fairground that people throw sticks or balls at, not a target for timid people

explanation.surface: A woman seems to be fair game for the bashful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shy' looks like timid but means throw, and 'fair' looks like just but is a fairground. AUNT SALLY is a traditional British pub and fair game of throwing at a dummy's head; by extension, anyone set up as an easy target of criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: The figure is literally the target thrown at in the fairground game, and figuratively someone everyone takes aim at.

clue.text: The underworld business of musical entertainment

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and the name of the underworld itself
Co is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: Organised crime runs a firm that stages shows with music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The underworld' suggests gangsters, but it is DIS, the classical realm of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is an evening of dancing to recorded pop music, a form of musical entertainment.

clue.text: Confound the pitch!

definitions.meaning: to confound someone is to disconcert or baffle them, as a tricky question can do
to pitch is to hurl or toss something

explanation.surface: A frustrated cry cursing a football field or cricket wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confound the pitch!' reads as an oath against a playing field, but 'pitch' is a verb meaning hurl.
explanation.definitionFit: A surprise can disconcert you, and to hurl a ball is to toss it: one word covers both senses.

clue.text: Suffering blows in turns, broke down in tears

parts.note: winds means turns, as a road winds
wept means cried, broke down in tears

explanation.surface: Someone beaten repeatedly finally cried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suffering blows' sounds like being hit, but means exposed to strong winds.
explanation.definitionFit: A windswept place is exposed to gales, buffeted by strong gusts.

clue.text: Conflict bombastically pronounced justified

parts.note: war is armed conflict
to rant is to speak in a loud, bombastic way, so ranted means pronounced bombastically

explanation.surface: A war hawk declared loudly that the fighting had been right.
explanation.definitionFit: Something warranted is supported by good reason, so it is deserved and justified.

clue.text: Contemplates what's odd in a set-up?

parts.note: rum is old British slang for odd or strange
taken as written

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, means the word set is written bottom to top, backwards

explanation.surface: A person ponders what is peculiar about an arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set-up' reads as an arrangement, but 'up' turns SET into TES. RUM is British slang for strange.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruminate is to think deeply, to contemplate, like a cow chewing cud.

clue.text: This town has not put up overpass

indicators.note: put up, in a down clue, means the little word is written upwards, backwards

parts.note: a bridge is an overpass

explanation.surface: A town is said to lack a raised road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns NOT into TON. TONBRIDGE is a town in Kent, south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonbridge is a market town in Kent, England.

clue.text: Study with a Parisian one way to beat a problem

parts.note: to con is an old word meaning to study or learn by heart
un is French for a, as a Parisian would say it
to drum is one way of beating, with fingers or sticks

explanation.surface: A student works with a Frenchman to find a method of solving a hard question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat a problem' reads as solve it, but 'one way to beat' is DRUM and 'problem' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A conundrum is a puzzling question or riddle, a difficult problem.

clue.text: Blush about skirts being worn

parts.note: c is circa, about
to skirt is to border, and rims are borders, so skirts means rims
clothes that are on are being worn

explanation.surface: Someone goes red about their skirts being worn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skirts' looks like clothing but is RIMS, edges.
explanation.definitionFit: Crimson is a deep red, and as a verb means to turn red, to blush.

clue.text: Dance with beat and energy

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
go is energy or vigour, as in full of go

explanation.surface: Someone dances with rhythm and vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat' suggests rhythm in a dance, but here it is TAN, to thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a ballroom dance from Argentina.

clue.text: Ham on the turn

parts.note: over means on, concerning, as in a row over money
a turn is an act on stage, as in a variety turn

explanation.surface: Meat that is going off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the turn' reads as milk or meat going off, but it is OVER (on) plus ACT (a stage turn). 'Ham' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham is to overplay a part on stage, with exaggerated acting.

clue.text: 'olders of belief current in Asia

indicators.note: the apostrophe in place of a first letter mimics Cockney speech, which drops the aitch from words

parts.note: holders of a belief here are followers of a faith of India

explanation.surface: A dropped-aitch remark about believers and a stream in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe before 'olders' copies Cockney speech, which drops H; so the H goes from the word for followers of the Hindu faith, written in full as the aitch-dropped word implies.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indus is a great river of Pakistan, and a river is a current of water.

clue.text: Exhaust pipe

definitions.meaning: to exhaust is to use up or deplete, as resources are worn away
a pipe or channel carrying away waste water

explanation.surface: A car's tailpipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhaust pipe' reads as part of a car; split it into two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: It means both to deplete energy and a channel for waste water.

clue.text: Crowd not in favour of hunting

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
to course is to hunt game, especially hares, with hounds that chase by sight

explanation.surface: A mob of people opposed to blood sports.
explanation.walkthrough: COURSING is hare hunting with greyhounds, once common in Britain; the verb 'course' means hunt in this way.
explanation.definitionFit: A concourse is a throng of people gathered together, a crowd.

clue.text: Nasty creature fellow caught turned over

indicators.note: turned over says the whole run of letters is flipped, read backwards

parts.note: a peer is an equal, a fellow
c is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A vile animal has captured a man and flipped him over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned over' reverses PEER then C together.
explanation.definitionFit: A creep is an unpleasant, obnoxious person.

clue.text: Nothing that is side-splitting occurs in this college

parts.note: O is zero, nothing

indicators.note: splitting means one piece pushes in between the parts of another

parts.note: R and L, right and left, each a side
ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: Zero hilarity in a certain college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'side-splitting' reads as hilarious, but IE splits R and L (right, left). ORIEL is a college of Oxford University.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriel College is one of the colleges of Oxford University.

clue.text: Account given in New Testament

indicators.note: New signals the letters of the word that follows are made new, rearranged

explanation.surface: A story told in the Christian scriptures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Testament' reads as the Bible, but 'New' is the anagram signal for TESTAMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement is a formal account of facts or events, as given to the police.

clue.text: Service, given backing, succeeds in the country

indicators.note: succeeds means comes after, so the turned piece follows the next word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: given backing means the word for service is written backwards

parts.note: aid is help or service given

explanation.surface: Military service, with support, pays off within a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given backing' reverses the word for service; 'succeeds' means that reversed piece comes after the word in.
explanation.definitionFit: India is a country of South Asia.

clue.text: Express without punctuation

definitions.meaning: an express train runs through without stopping
read literally, a text with no stops, the full stops of punctuation

explanation.surface: A speedy train, or writing with no full stops.
explanation.walkthrough: A full stop is a punctuation mark, so text with no stops at all is literally this.
explanation.definitionFit: An express service does not halt between ends, and unpunctuated text has no full stops.

clue.text: Prominent overseas visitor getting in the way

indicators.note: getting in tells us one word goes inside another

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
an alien is a foreigner, a visitor from overseas

explanation.surface: A notable foreigner is causing an obstruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting in the way' reads as obstructing, but 'getting in' is the container signal and 'the way' is a street.
explanation.definitionFit: Salient means most noticeable or important, standing out.
